phases.title: Before the doors open
phases.goal: Remove what costs something on every request, cold start, scheduled run or agent session, with small and safe changes, and make the changes that are cheapest while no real store, order or picture exists. No step here waits for the owner's answer or for a later phase. Steps 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.43 go first; 0.43 comes before 0.6, 0.9 and 0.38, 0.23 before 0.24, 0.9 before 0.11, 0.28 before 0.29, and 0.33 before 0.44. Otherwise no step waits for another.
phases.notice: Almost nothing on a screen changes, apart from two faults a shopper would have met on day one (empty search thumbnails, and a button with no fill on the status and report pages) and admin lists that show 100 rows at a time. Cold pages answer sooner, an admin screen loads about half the script, a store page stops asking the server for a wishlist and stock nobody has, and the database falls from 731 MB to about 230 MB.

steps.title: Put the review's scripts and lists in the repo
steps.what: The detectors this plan's checks name exist only in the review's scratch folder: the refined copy counter, the twin counter, the import-reach walker, the trace summers and four deletion lists. Copy them to docs/audits/bloat-review-2026-11/scripts/ and lists/, beside the seven scripts already there, and point every done-when at the repo path. Do this first: steps 0.6, 0.8 and 0.36 are proved with these scripts, and phase 1 turns them into tests. It also moves into the repo every script a bar or a done-when names: the four cold-load scripts, flight.mjs and route.mjs, the reader of the build's .meta files, the copy, twin and helper counters, words-in-entries.mjs, handed.mjs, the manifest timer, the admin's cut simulation and the AI round's draw. And it commits this plan as a tracker: a Progress table with one row a step, and one section per step under a heading that starts with its id.
steps.done_when: Each script, run with node from a fresh checkout, gives its number again (41 twin pairs, 4,098 exact copied lines across files, 1,308 files reached by /api/visit), no bar and no done-when names a path under the scratchpad or work/ (rg -n 'scratchpad|work/' over this plan, its cards and the findings files prints nothing), and the plan's tracker under docs/audits/bloat-review-2026-11 has one Progress row and one section for each step.
steps.platform: The scripts read the whole of src, so the platform's files and routes are counted with the stores'.

steps.title: Store a daily reading of production, so every later step has a 'before'
steps.what: Production's statistics are read by hand and no reading is kept. Add one statement to the daily route (src/app/api/cron/subscription-reminders/route.ts). It writes a dated reading into a small platform table, kept 90 days. The reading holds the 40 costliest and the 40 most-called statements of the app's role (Postgres has already stripped the values), each commerce table's rows, size and scan counters, and the size of each schema. No screen yet: step 1.13 shows the reading and adds the flags, and closes the gap this step starts on. Land it before the fixes, so their 'before' is on record.
steps.done_when: In production the new table holds two days of readings before step 0.23 is deployed, and an int test shows the daily statement writing one row for each commerce table and at most 80 statement rows.
steps.platform: The reading is the platform's own table, and it counts Kaizena Flow's store and its null-store rows with every other.

steps.title: Let the deploy job, not a visitor, meet the first cold page
steps.what: scripts/await-deploy.mjs waits for /api/health and stops. Add page checks from SMOKE_PAGES (Kaizena Flow's home and one page of the template store), so the job pays the first draw and a page that answers 500 fails the run. prerenderedShops() also returns the house store's markets while the switch is on, so kaizenaflow.com is built with each deploy, and CI seeds a house store with the switch on. The review measured Kaizena Flow's front page in a form production no longer serves: measure production's again and write it into docs/performance.md. Land this before steps 0.4 to 0.8: each of them changes what loads cold, and this is the check that catches a missed import in production.
steps.done_when: src/lib/await-deploy.test.ts shows that a page answering 500 fails the job, and after a deploy the release job's log lists Kaizena Flow's home and one template-store page with status 200, their bytes, and the cache header of a prerendered page.
steps.platform: Kaizena Flow's own front page is the first page checked, and it is prerendered with every deploy.

steps.what: src/db/client.ts hands the 19,614-line Drizzle schema to a query builder nobody calls, so 481 table definitions are built at every cold start: make the import type-only and call drizzle({ client: pool }), three lines. The four /api/visit beacons, /api/recommendations/events and /api/docs/feedback take sameSite and two more small helpers through src/server/chat-route.ts, which brings the chat, the AI layer and the support desk with it: import them from the files that define them. /api/recommendations/events also takes visitorKey from src/server/chat-turns.ts, not through chat-agent.ts. In the same change correct the note on the Postgres driver in the code review's dependency item.

steps.title: Make a language translated by AI cost what it uses: at start, per document and per minute
steps.what: The start hook (src/instrumentation.ts) loads 856 modules, among them the translating tools, ai.ts and auth.ts, then reads every AI-translated language whole before the first request, and each instance polls the table every minute. Split the interface-text reader from the translating tools. Read at start with two statements, whatever the number of languages, and build a language on first read. Poll a one-row version stamp every ten minutes, only where such a language is served. uiTextsFor() sends the browser its 114 texts, not all 1,673: 93 KB to under 9 KB in every document of such a store. The search-cache prune that the same finding names leaves the five-minute list in step 0.31.

steps.what: Screens and polls that only draw a button fetch the whole AI connection, key and month's cost included: 12.4 reads for each AI call made. Give them aiAbilities() from a 60-second memo with no key. Sum the month's AI cost from daily rows plus today (37 to 57 ms a call now). A job reads the connection once per run. steps.title: Filter a store's rows the way its index can serve
steps.what: Postgres cannot answer store_id is not distinct from $1 from an index, so the hottest reads scan every store's rows: about 1.2 billion rows in 78 days on pages, cookie_scans and terms (122 uses in 40 files). One owned() helper writes store_id = $1 for a store and store_id is null for the platform, and the ratchet counts the old wording per file. The cookie scan's every-minute due check gets two indexes on the expression it filters by, and a failing site backs off. Do it before the new page reads of steps 0.24 and 2.16 are written, so they are born right. This rewrites the filter that keeps stores apart, so the order is fixed: land owned() first, with a unit test for a store id and for the null owner; then move the 122 uses file by file, each with its integration tests; and place a test order after the deploy.
steps.done_when: The ratchet's count of 'store_id is not distinct from' in src/server is at most 3 commented column-to-column lines (122 today); a unit test of owned() covers a store id and the null owner, and each moved file's integration tests pass unchanged; a plan test on a seeded table of 200 owners shows store_id in the Index Cond of the page list, the page by address, the page names and the modal statement, for a store and for a null owner; and in production seq_scan of commerce.cookie_scans grows by fewer than 1,000 a day (fewer than 10 once step 3.1 is in), with scheduled cookie scans a day at most a seventh of the sites plus 5.
steps.platform: The is-null branch of owned() is the platform's: its pages, terms and cookie scans are found by index too.

steps.title: Read one page, not all of them
steps.what: listPublishedPages() (src/server/pages.ts) selects every published page of a store with its whole content. steps.what: Not one number of the checks is held, while the production build peaks at about 7.2 GB of 8. scripts/timed.mjs wraps lint, the type check, the unit run, each integration shard, each Playwright run and each build, with ceilings in scripts/ci-budgets.json (25% above the median of the last ten runs, 10% for the build's memory; no single run of a job a release waits for over 10 minutes). A check fails when a CI step runs outside the recorder. scripts/next-build.mjs prints seconds and peak memory after every build, Vercel's included; scripts/await-deploy.mjs writes the seconds from push to live, and Playwright's JSON reporter gives the tests that passed only on a retry. Measure both source-map switches under an 8 GB cap before anything is paid for (about 4.7 MB of heap per MB of server code), and write their rows into docs/build-memory.md: if the peak is 6.0 GB or less, the purchase of step 1.21 can wait. The recorder labels lint and the type check warm or cold, with a ceiling for each, and prints install seconds per job and the push's runner-minutes, with a ceiling on the sum. A weekly workflow goes red when a ceiling is more than 25% above the median of the last ten runs. pnpm check runs the pre-push rule through the recorder. It holds the build's measures 4, 6 and 7.
steps.done_when: Every CI run's summary lists seconds for lint and the type check (labelled warm or cold), the unit run, each shard, each browser job and the build, install seconds per job, the push's runner-minutes, the build's peak memory, the seconds from push to live and the retried tests. A run fails above a ceiling in scripts/ci-budgets.json; scripts/timed.mjs fails when setup passes 10% of the unit run or the files run differ from the files on disk; a CI step run outside the recorder fails a check; pnpm check prints the same seconds in a session; and docs/build-memory.md has a row for each source-map setting, measured under an 8 GB cap. Five planted cases turn a test or a run red and name the cause.

steps.title: Only if the free switches are not enough: build in CI and deploy the prebuilt output
steps.what: Stage 2 of the build's room, split out of step 1.21: make the production build in CI and deploy it prebuilt. Today (.github/workflows/ci.yml, docs/ci-migrations.md) the pending job, for a push with no migration, runs the quick gate, calls Vercel's deploy hook and waits on /api/health; the release job, for a push with a migration, waits for every check, applies the files, calls the same hook and waits. Vercel then builds the head of main on its own machine. In stage 2 the hook call in both jobs becomes three commands in the same job and the same place: vercel pull --environment=production, vercel build --prod, vercel deploy --prebuilt --prod. So a migration is still applied before the build that needs it is deployed, a failed gate or migration still deploys nothing, and scripts/await-deploy.mjs still waits for the commit and runs its checks. Four things must be made true, and tried on a preview deployment before production. (1) /api/health reports VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA (src/lib/health.ts:82). If a prebuilt deployment leaves it empty, the build writes GITHUB_SHA into its output and health reads that. (2) vercel build sets VERCEL, so next.config.ts's ON_VERCEL limits (one worker, no build cache, no type check) would follow the build to CI. Key the worker and cache limits on the machine that builds, and bring the cache and the extra workers back only if a build stays at 75% of the runner or less. The type check stays out of this build: the gate has run it on the same commit. (3) The prebuilt output is this run's commit, not the head of main as the hook builds today (D530). The check for a migration pending at the head goes, and an order guard comes: read /api/health just before the deploy, and skip it when production already runs a commit that includes this one, so an older build never lands on a newer one. (4) Three free secrets in GitHub: a Vercel token and the project's two ids. Production's settings reach the runner through vercel pull and are never printed; production's database address is already a secret there for the migrations. The deploy hook stays for the manual redeploy job, as the way back. What the review found about the runner: CI's e2e, hosts and signed-in jobs already run pnpm build with the type check inside on ubuntu-latest and pass, a setup docs/build-memory.md records as killed under 8 GB, and this review's build peaked at 7.61 GB with the type check, the cache and all workers on. So the runner has more room than Vercel's machine, but its size, and whether the repository is private, were not read: the review had no GitHub access. Before stage 2, print the runner's memory and cores in a run and write them into docs/build-memory.md, and read the repository's visibility and its Actions usage. On a public repository minutes are free. On a private one they are metered: stop and tell the owner if a month's minutes would rise. CI's own test builds cannot be the deployed one: they are built on the seeded test database with test addresses compiled in. The production build is therefore one more build of about 4 to 5 minutes (263 s measured in this review), run inside the job that already has the checkout and the install, and it takes the place of Vercel's own build, so the time from push to live does not grow. Steps 0.38 and 3.18 take three type checks and one build out of every push, which is more than this adds, so stage 2 comes after step 0.38 and the push's runner-minutes end no higher than before. If docs/build-memory.md says 'Stage 1 is enough' after step 1.21, this step changes nothing and is set to Done as not needed.
steps.done_when: Either docs/build-memory.md says 'Stage 1 is enough' and this step is Done as not needed; or ten production builds in a row peak at 75% of the runner's printed size or less, one push with a migration and one without each reach production through vercel deploy --prebuilt with /api/health reporting the commit, a run whose commit production already includes deploys nothing, and the recorder shows the median runner-minutes of a push no higher than before the move. No paid machine or plan is used.

phases.title: Load on demand
phases.goal: The structural half: each page, function, document and AI call loads what it uses, when it uses it. Before opening is the cheapest time for it, and phase 1's budgets show each step as a number that falls. Order where it matters: 2.2 before 2.3, 2.4 before 2.5, 2.14 before 2.15, 2.16 before 2.17 and 2.18, 2.20 before 2.35, 2.36 before 2.37, 2.27 and 2.29 before 2.30, 1.21 before 2.11, 2.11 before 2.49, 2.25 and 2.26 before 2.50, and 2.9 and 2.22 before 2.47. Step 2.1 is first because it only waits for the owner's yes.
phases.notice: A store page arrives as a static file with nothing in it twice. A product view asks the database for stock and nothing else. A publish redraws one page, not the whole store. Admin screens hand the browser only the words they show, and the builder paints before its editors load. The AI manager answers on a third of the tokens. With the owner's yes, an agent session starts with a quarter of today's standing rules.

steps.title: Leave a map in CLAUDE.md, and bring the always-loaded core under 10.5 KB
steps.what: Every session and subagent loads CLAUDE.md's 295-line feature index (43,361 bytes in all), of which a change needs two to four lines. Replace it with a map of the seven rule files and a three-line look-up, and change src/lib/rules-index.test.ts so it no longer asks for a line per rule: that takes the file under 15 KB. Then move the database, e2e, typed-row and AI-eval how-to into .claude/rules files loaded by path, where a fresh session and a subagent are shown to receive them; otherwise they sit in docs/rules as rules read on demand. Every sentence that guards an action taken without opening a file stays in the core. The docs budget of step 1.1 then holds 10,500 bytes and 160 lines as a hard ceiling. The owner has said yes to both halves. It is the largest saving per agent session in the plan. The commit message lists each block that left CLAUDE.md and the file that now holds it, so the owner can read what changed in his instruction file.
steps.done_when: wc -c -l CLAUDE.md prints under 10,500 bytes and 160 lines (43,361 and 448 today) with every never-sentence still in it, src/lib/rules-index.test.ts passes, a fresh session that opens src/db/client.ts can quote the database rule's first sentence, and the proof of path loading is also run in a subagent, or the text stays in docs/rules.

steps.asked: CLAUDE.md is your instruction file. First: may its 295-line feature index go, leaving a map of the seven rule files and a three-line look-up (44 KB to under 15 KB per session)? Second, and it can be declined on its own: may the database, e2e, typed-row and AI-eval how-to load only when those folders are opened (to under 10.5 KB)? Without the first yes the rules area cannot reach a B; without the second it stops short of an A, at the 15 KB ceiling.
steps.decision: Yes to both halves. The 295-line feature index leaves CLAUDE.md for a map of the seven rule files and a three-line look-up, and the database, e2e, typed-row and AI-eval how-to load only when their folders are opened; the critic says the rules area needs both for an A. Every never-sentence stays in the file.

steps.title: Bound what a real listing fetches ahead, and decide partial prefetching by trial
steps.what: A real listing prefetches every product tile and up to six swatch links under each: about 96 requests for 48 products, and the test stores are too small to show it. Seed a 48-product category and bound it at 20 router requests read to the end, with swatches on intent. Run the partial-prefetching trial on the product page, the seeded listing, the store home and the admin's orders page, and write its table into docs/performance.md and the decision into docs/decisions.md: the first screen of tiles is fetched on sight and the rest on touch, unless the trial shows that one shared shell for all links to a route does clearly better; then the shell replaces it. The next major Next release forces the choice.
steps.done_when: e2e/prefetch.spec.ts holds the seeded 48-product category read to the end on a phone at no more than 20 router requests, and docs/performance.md holds the trial's before-and-after table with the decision recorded in docs/decisions.md.
steps.platform: The trial's fourth page is an admin page, so the choice is made for /admin/platform's lists too.
steps.asked: On a full listing, may only the first screen of product tiles be fetched ahead on sight, and the rest when touched (or all through one shared product shell)? A yes lets the shopper's browser reach an A.
steps.decision: Yes. On a full listing only the first screen of product tiles is fetched ahead on sight and the rest when touched, and on a computer the main menu's links wait for the pointer (step 2.6 sets that policy); the critic says the shopper's browser needs this for an A. The trial decides whether one shared product shell replaces the rule; without a clear gain the first-screen rule stands, since it needs no router setting.

steps.what: One tag, pages:{store}, covers all of a store's pages, and 55 places refresh it: one publish makes all 261 built pages of the demo render again. steps.title: Give every table that grows by time a delete rule
steps.what: Seven tables grow by time with no delete: guest carts, processed webhook events, email messages, experiment events, referral visits, Work events and old page versions. Each gets a period in src/lib/retention.ts and a delete step in the daily run; the privacy text states the same periods. The periods: a guest cart goes 90 days after it ended (an open cart: after its expiry), unless an order points at it; the rule 'carts' in src/lib/retention.ts reads '90 days ... After the cart ended (an open cart: its expiry).' A processed webhook event goes, row and all, 90 days after it was processed; the rule 'webhook_payloads' reads '90 days ... After the event was processed; the row stays so its id still de-duplicates', so before that delete lands an int test shows that an event delivered again after its row is gone changes nothing, and a kind of event for which that cannot be shown keeps its rows. A page keeps all 50 versions for 90 days and then its newest 10 (VERSIONS_KEPT in src/lib/page-versions.ts is 50, with no age rule today), and the Versions panel says so. The other four take the period of the nearest rule the file already states: an email message's row 12 months after its body was emptied (the rule 'email_bodies' is 12 months), experiment events and referral visits 25 months (as 'visits'), Work events 24 months (as 'audit_log'). These deletes remove production rows for good. Before the push that turns them on: take a dump of the seven tables, restore it to a scratch database and compare the row counts table by table, keep it with the backups, and show the owner where the dump is and how many rows the first run will delete in each table. The push waits until the owner has seen them. The status prune leaves the five-minute tick for the daily route. The docs index rewrites only the rows that changed, not all 1,845 on every docs deploy. The seven are the known ones; nothing says the next table has a rule. A register puts every commerce table in one of four classes: kept with its parent, deleted after a stated period, kept for the law, or reference data. The tables are counted from the migrations (486).
steps.done_when: src/lib/retention.test.ts finds a delete step for every table that grows by time, in production seq_scan of commerce.status_checks grows by fewer than 10 a day (about 288 today), and a deploy that changes one docs article raises n_tup_upd of commerce.docs_index by fewer than 50 (1,845 before); and a scan test fails for a commerce table in no class, for a 'deleted after' table with no period in src/lib/retention.ts and no delete step, and on a scratch table with a created_at column and no class. The privacy text and the Versions panel state the periods of src/lib/retention.ts and src/lib/page-versions.ts, and the owner has seen the dump and the first run's row counts before the deletes were pushed.
steps.platform: The status page, the docs index and the platform's webhook events are the platform's own tables and get their periods in the same file.
steps.asked: How long are guest carts, processed webhook events and old page versions kept (the code review's question 6)? The privacy text states the same periods.
steps.decision: The periods the repo already states are used. A guest cart is deleted 90 days after it ended (an open cart: after its expiry), unless an order points at it, and a processed webhook event 90 days after it was processed: src/lib/retention.ts:180 and :184 and docs/wave-1g-gdpr.md:287 and :291 state those periods, and today the rows are only emptied at that age. A page keeps all 50 versions for 90 days and then its newest 10, the finding's rule, because an unbounded history would in time need a larger database.
